messages.author: 86f142026011386f
messages.subject: viewing columns and rows
parts:
Hey everybody

I have quite a large table of something like 50 columns and 400 rows.

I used
Alldata=read.table("survey_44792_data_file_20091204.csv", sep=",",
quote = "'", na.strings='""')
1. Now I want to address a specific column, is it automatically ranged
as V1... Vn ?

2. I read that I should use scan instead of read.table, does it make
such a big different ?

3. Is there a command that let me view my Alldata in a simple way or
should i use an exterior program like excell to look at .csv file ?
thnx
asaf.

messages.author: a305e65fa9dfb74d
messages.subject: Re: viewing columns and rows
parts:
1. If your data has no column labels, you can access columns either by their names (V1,V2,...) or location. Try names( ) to check for the names. More information is here:
http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-intro.html#Index-vectors

2. If the loading time didn't bother you, no reason to try scan( ).
A very good manual for importing data can be found here:
http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/R-data.html

3. While not recommended for big data files, print( ) and edit( ) will do the trick.

I hope this helps

Jonathan

messages.subject: Re: viewing columns and rows
parts:
Regarding cbind VS data.frame
If you where to connect variables of the same type, cbind will bind them into a matrix (as Jonathan wrote).
There are more differences, I believe doing:
?cbind
?data.frame
Should help.

Regarding changing variable names, I would use:
colnames(dataframe.name) <- c(a vector of new variable names)


Cheers,
Tal

parts:
Moreover, the difference between "cbind" and "data.frame" has more to do with data types:

cbind creates matrices (i.e only one data type - numbers, text, etc). If you try to join different data types together R will convert them into the most permissive data type of the group. the hierarchy is boolean -> integer -> double -> text, so joining anything to a text vector with cbind will convert it into text (see example below).
  
data.frame creates - well - data frames which can contain different data types.

example:

x = cbind(number = c(1:3), text = c("a","b","c"))
print(x)
sum(x[,'number'])         # error - can't sum text

x = data.frame(number = c(1:3), text = c("a","b","c"))
print(x)
sum(x[,'number'])        # this time it works

Yizhar
